cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: The EU began as the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951 and evolved into a political and economic union of 27 member states cooperating on trade, law, and policy.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: The UK joined the European Communities in 1973. A 1975 referendum confirmed membership with 67% voting to stay in. Membership gave access to the single market and freedom of movement.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: The 2016 EU referendum result: 51.9% voted Leave, 48.1% voted Remain. Turnout was 72.2%. England and Wales voted Leave; Scotland and Northern Ireland voted Remain.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: Key Leave arguments: regaining parliamentary sovereignty (making all UK laws in the UK), controlling immigration (ending freedom of movement), making independent trade deals, and saving EU budget contributions (£17.4bn gross in 2019).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: Key Remain arguments: economic benefits of the single market (access to 450 million consumers), freedom to live and work across the EU, cooperation on security and the environment, and the EU's role in maintaining peace in Europe.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty triggered the formal leaving process on 29 March 2017. The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020 and the transition period ended on 31 December 2020.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: The Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) governs UK-EU relations post-Brexit: tariff-free trade for most goods (if rules of origin are met), but new customs checks and regulatory barriers.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: Brexit affected: trade (new barriers and costs), travel (passports required, 90-day limit in Schengen area), citizens' rights (EU Settlement Scheme for EU nationals in the UK), and the Northern Ireland border (the Protocol and Windsor Framework).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: The UK still follows many EU-derived laws but can now diverge from them. The Retained EU Law Act 2023 provides a mechanism for amending or removing these laws.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: The long-term economic and political effects of Brexit continue to be debated. The OBR estimated it would reduce UK GDP by about 4% long-term compared to EU membership.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: Young people aged 16-17 could not vote in the referendum (unlike the Scottish independence referendum), which many argue was unfair given they would live with the consequences longest.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The EU & Brexit
cards.back: Post-Brexit, the UK has joined the CPTPP (Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership) and negotiated bilateral trade deals with Australia, Japan, and others.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — the eu & brexit?
cards.back: 1. For The EU & Brexit questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link The EU & Brexit to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
